top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P001) still best meets the test of a voice heard in this writing and nowhere else, where formal ambition and imaginative depth are the same thing. On public knowledge and the longlist description, which I have not independently verified, memory, the body and dream are the structural principle of the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, not just their subject. The late novels appear to extend an earlier project, which bears on sustained quality. Attribution is clean: one writer, writing in Romanian. I keep the citation scoped to the prose project, with poetry only as formative ground, because my coverage of the poetry and early fiction is partial. The case is conditional. I judge through translation, so I cannot confirm that the very long late books earn their length rather than letting scale stand in for structure. I apply the same translation standard to all three leading candidates. Carson (P003) is second: her English text is directly legible and Sward's continuity argument has narrowed my doubts, but I still cannot tell how evenly the smaller books are sustained or how a text-only citation would handle the book-object work. Adonis (P002) is third. Remaking a literary language is a major achievement, but I cannot vouch for the later poetry without Arabic readers, and that is a limit of my evidence, not a judgment against him. P000 is last because the evidence for all three leading candidates is serious enough to warrant an award.
